title: Examining the impact of sharing COVID-19 misinformation online on mental health
screen_reason: The paper's aim is causal (effect of sharing COVID-19 misinformation on anxiety), but the sample-description section reports a verbatim numerator and denominator for the share of Twitter users classified as misinformation sharers: 'out of the 43,832 users, 1,288 users were assigned to the treatment group'. That is an observed, behavioural share of users who shared misinformation (SHARING / actor_share), so the paper is eligible under the rule that a study whose aim is something else is still included if a descriptive share is reported.

estimates.country: Not stated (Twitter users posting about COVID-19; a US-located subset is analysed separately)
estimates.measure_type: % of active Twitter users in a COVID-19 tweet panel who shared at least five COVID-19 misinformative posts (classifier-labelled)
estimates.denominator: 43,832 Twitter users who posted about COVID-19 at least once between 1 Jan 2019 and 15 Jul 2020 and survived the inactive-account filter
estimates.definition: A user counted in the numerator if the ULMFiT classifier labelled at least five of their posts as COVID-19 misinformation (claims about vitamins/minerals curing COVID-19, gargling warm water, 5G, tap water spreading the virus, the virus as a biological weapon, Bill Gates creating the virus)
estimates.misinfo_def: “Misinformation is defined as information that has the features of being false or incorrectly presented, whether intentionally or not, determined based on expert evidence and shared with no intention of harm”
estimates.source_quote: Using this assignment technique, out of the 43,832 users, 1,288 users were assigned to the treatment group and 31,002 users were assigned to the control group.
estimates.page_loc: Methods, 'Creating control and treatment groups', p. 3
estimates.ground_truth_detail: ULMFiT large language model fine-tuned in two stages on the manually-labelled COVID-19 misinformation data of Micallef et al. (2020); precision 0.90 at a classification threshold of 0.70. Bot accounts estimated at <2.0% of all subcategories.
estimates.moderator_quote: We started with the dataset curated by Micallef et al.46 comprising 76,985 users who made Twitter posts at least once about COVID-19 during the above time period. We adopted filtering steps to remove inactive accounts, which resulted in the timelines of 43,832 Twitter users.
estimates.notes: The share is an exact part/whole from two verbatim counts in the same sentence (1,288 of 43,832). IMPORTANT CAVEAT for the adjudicator: the numerator uses a >=5-misinformative-posts threshold chosen empirically for the causal design, not 'shared any misinformation', so this understates the share of users who shared any misinformation and is not comparable to a standard actor_share. borderline=true is set for that reason. Year of data collection spans 2019-2020; 2020 recorded because the COVID-19 misinformation exposure period falls in 2020.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) The paper also states verbatim that '31,002 users were assigned to the control group' (users who shared NO misinformation), i.e. 31,002/43,832 = 70.7% shared none. The corresponding 'shared at least one misinformative post' figure (29.3%) is a complement I would have to compute, which R8 forbids, so it is not extracted; an adjudicator may wish to know that 11,542 users (43,832 - 32,290) shared between one and four misinformative posts and were placed in neither group. 2) All other reported numbers are treatment effects, not prevalence shares: relative treatment effect 2.011, Cohen's d 0.59, threshold-sensitivity values TE_rel = 1.082 (threshold 3) and 4.639 (threshold 7), and the socio-demographic relative anxiety increases (women 163.4%, men 151.72%, whites 169.6%, Blacks 207.5%, APIs 237.31%, Hispanics 205.65%). These are percentage increases in anxiety, not shares of misinformation, and are excluded. 3) '<2.0%' bot accounts is a share of bots, not of misinformation. 4) The 80 million posts / 30 million analysed posts are counts with no misinformation numerator reported at post level, so no CONTENT row is possible.

rob.design: Observational Twitter panel; frame = 76,985 users who posted about COVID-19 at least once between 1 Jan 2019 and 15 Jul 2020 (dataset of Micallef et al.), filtered for inactivity to 43,832 users and ~40 million posts; no response rate (behavioural trace data). Misinformation coded by a fine-tuned ULMFiT classifier trained on manually-labelled data, precision 0.90 at threshold 0.70; anxiety scored by a separate classifier with ~0.90 held-out accuracy; bots <2.0%. No human inter-coder reliability statistic reported for the misinformation labels in the main text.
